1422.title: Nirvana Day again
1422.howItsDone: In Japan and other East Asian communities, temples keep Nirvana Day with chanting, sutra reading and a painted scroll of the passing; in Theravada lands the passing is remembered on Vesak together with the birth and the awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rohatsu, a week of sitting that ends at the morning star. Your line was the morning star.

A doctor comes home from a long trip and finds his children rolling on the floor. While he was away, they drank poison. Some still have their wits, and take the medicine he mixes. The others, their minds turned, won't touch it. So the doctor does something strange. He leaves again, and sends word home: your father is dead. You met it in the Lotus Sutra this year; it returns on Nirvana Day, the day the Buddha's passing is remembered, because the Lotus tells it about that very passing.
screen: `CHILDREN WHO DRANK POISON.` → `THEY REFUSE THE MEDICINE.` → `YOUR FATHER IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: On day six ninety-two you met the scene the schools share: the Buddha lying down between two sal trees at Kusinara, and his last instruction, which in paraphrase says that everything put together comes apart, so keep going with care. First, the Pali texts the Theravada keeps. A short book of sayings, the Itivuttaka, speaks of two elements of nibbana. One is nibbana with something remaining: an awakened person still alive, still feeling pleasant and painful things, but with greed, hatred and delusion gone. The other is nibbana with nothing remaining, when that life ends and all that was felt simply grows cool. The passing is real and complete: a fire gone out. Second, the Lotus Sutra. In its chapter on the lifespan of the Tathagata, the Buddha says he awoke immeasurable ages ago, and that his passing is a skillful means. In plain sight forever, people would grow careless. Like the doctor, he appears to go. In their grief the children come to their senses and drink the medicine. Then, the story says, the father comes home. Third, the Diamond Sutra, near its end: the Tathagata doesn't come from anywhere and doesn't go anywhere, and that, it says, is why he is called the Tathagata. Each school explains its own reading, and this path doesn't rank them. Some hear one thing shared with those last words: each ending is put to work, to wake the ones still here. Even where the Buddha never really left, the ending has to look real, or nobody takes the medicine.
screen: `TWO ELEMENTS OF NIBBANA.` · `THE DOCTOR SEEMS TO LEAVE.` · `NEITHER COMING NOR GOING.` · then, large: `AN ENDING THAT WAKES.`

segments.voice: Let three or four out-breaths finish completely. Then let one ending from this past year come to mind, a job, a home, a friend who moved away, and ask it the doctor's question: did this ending wake anything up? Don't push for an answer; if sadness comes, let it sit beside you, and if grief ever feels like too much to carry alone, you can call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Nirvana Day. The day remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana, kept on different calendars and read in different ways by the schools. Today's word.
Your line: all things end. And some endings wake the ones still here. See you tomorrow, for Losar.

1423.title: Losar again
1423.howItsDone: Tibetans and Himalayan Buddhist communities keep Losar by the lunar calendar with house cleaning, new prayer flags, family visits, offerings of barley flour and grain, and monastery rituals; in the first month, monasteries in some places also hold Monlam prayer gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirvana Day: a fire gone out, a doctor who seemed to leave, a coming and going that was neither. Your line was all things end.

A guest steps into a Tibetan home on new year's morning, and before anything else, someone holds out a wooden box, split in two. One side is heaped with roasted barley flour, the other with barley grain, stalks of grain standing up like little flags. The guest tosses a pinch into the air, then another, then a third, and puts a pinch on the tongue. Then the greetings begin. This is Losar. You met its brooms and prayer flags back on day six ninety-three. Today, look at it with this year's Tibetan map in hand.
screen: `A BOX OF BARLEY.` → `A PINCH TOSSED UP.` → `A PINCH TASTED.`

segments.voice: In the Tibetan block, you met a way Tibetan teachers describe their path: three vehicles practiced together, not one after another. Renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path. Losar isn't a teaching on that map, but it can be walked through with one. First, letting go. In the last days of the old year, houses are scrubbed, and old dust and old troubles are carried out the door. That's the household version of renunciation: the old year is over, so you stop holding it. Second, sharing. The pinch of barley isn't kept. It's thrown up and out, an offering, before anyone eats. Then come the visits, the gifts, and the greeting tashi delek, wishing good fortune on whoever you meet. The fresh year starts by giving something away. Third, the diamond path. In the monasteries, the turn of the year brings rituals and chanting, and in some places masked dances. And in the first month, by tradition, comes the Great Prayer festival, Monlam Chenmo, which Tibetan histories say Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug school, began in Lhasa. Monks gather to pray for the world, and lay people come to offer lamps and food. Monlam means an aspiration prayer: a wish set out ahead of you. So the year begins with all three at once. Clear the corner. Throw the pinch. Set out the wish. None waits for the others to be finished, which is just what those teachers said about the vehicles.
screen: `THREE VEHICLES, PRACTICED TOGETHER.` · `LETTING GO: THE SCRUBBED HOUSE.` · `SHARING: THE PINCH THROWN UP.` · then, large: `THE WISH: THE GREAT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Picture one corner of your home, a shelf, a drawer, a spot by the door, and with a few breaths, see what's there from a year that's already over and decide what goes. With the next few breaths, think of one person who might use something you'd let go of. With the last few, set out one wish for the coming year, short and plain, as if you were writing it on a flag for the wind.
Losar. The Tibetan new year: houses cleaned, offerings shared, and in the monasteries, rituals and the Great Prayer. Today's word.
Your line: a fresh year. Letting go, sharing and a wish, all at once. See you tomorrow.

1424.title: Magha Puja again
1424.hook: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind
1424.howItsDone: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Buddhists keep Magha Puja on a full moon with temple visits, giving, precepts and an evening candlelit walk around the temple, often chanting the verses of the Ovada Patimokkha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Losar: the scrubbed house, the pinch of barley thrown up, the Great Prayer. Your line was a fresh year.

A Chan monk lives up in the branches of a pine tree, so the story goes, and people call him the Bird's Nest master. One day a governor named Bai Juyi, who is also a poet, stands underneath and calls up: that's a dangerous place to sit. The monk calls down: your seat is more dangerous than mine. Then the governor asks the big question. What is the heart of the Buddha's teaching? And the monk in the tree answers with a verse you met on day one fifty. Today is Magha Puja, the full moon of that verse.
screen: `A MONK IN A PINE TREE.` → `YOUR SEAT IS MORE DANGEROUS.` → `WHAT IS THE HEART OF IT?`

segments.voice: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Magha Puja remembers a gathering of monks and the short teaching the Buddha gave them. One of its verses sits in the Dhammapada, and in Max Müller's words it reads: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." You've walked around a temple with that verse before. This year brought two more homes for it. First, the Abhidhamma, where this year began. The Theravada's higher teaching sorts every moment of mind, and its first book opens its list of topics with one sorting: states that are skillful, unskillful, or neither. The Pali for skillful is kusala, the same word behind Müller's to do good. So the middle of the verse is also the Abhidhamma's first cut. Then Chan. In Chinese tradition the verse is called the shared precept of the seven Buddhas, which tradition says each Buddha of the past taught. The Bird's Nest master gives the governor the verse: do no evil, do good. The governor is unimpressed. A child of three knows that, he says. And the monk answers, in the story as the Chan records keep it: a child of three may be able to say it, but an old man of eighty can't manage to do it. The verse isn't hard to understand. It's hard to do, every day, and that's why each school keeps coming back to it as the heart of it.
screen: `ONE VERSE ON THE FULL MOON.` · `SKILLFUL, UNSKILLFUL, NEITHER.` · `THE PRECEPT OF THE SEVEN BUDDHAS.` · then, large: `EASY TO SAY, HARD TO DO.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle like a glass of water left alone, the verse's third part. When it's a little clearer, choose one small harm you'll skip, child-sized, something a three-year-old could understand, and one small good thing you'll do, also child-sized. Then let both rest, and come back to the clearing water.
Magha Puja. The full moon remembering the gathering of monks and the verse: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind, carried by Theravada, the Abhidhamma and Chan alike. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of it. Easy to say, hard to do. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1424 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE YEAR IN ONE SITTING.`

1425.title: The year in one sitting
1425.hook: Abhidhamma, the sutras, Zen, Pure Land, Tibet, the movements, the practices
1425.howItsDone: Some Buddhist communities close a period of study with a longer sitting and a look back over what was taught, ending with a dedication of merit to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Magha Puja, and a monk in a pine tree: easy to say, hard to do. Your line was the heart of it.

A man is asleep under a mango tree. A ripe mango thumps down beside his head. He wakes, opens his eyes, reaches out, picks it up, squeezes it, smells it, and eats it. That little scene, a commentary's simile for how a single moment of seeing unfolds, is near where this year began. Today, one sitting for the whole year, from the falling mango to the full moon of the heart.
screen: `A MAN ASLEEP UNDER A TREE.` → `A MANGO FALLS.` → `ONE SITTING FOR THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: It began with the Abhidhamma: the mind taken apart into moments, each arising and passing, colored by factors, held up by roots. Then the great vehicle: the bodhisattva, who seeks waking for the sake of all, and the perfections of giving, ethics, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom. The Diamond Sutra opened on an ordinary morning: the Buddha dresses, walks for alms, eats, washes his feet and sits down. The Lotus gave you a burning house, a jewel sewn into a sleeping man's coat, a doctor who seemed to leave. Vimalakirti lay sick in a small room that somehow held seats for a whole assembly, and answered a question with silence. Zen and Chan: a straight back, thumbs just touching, breaths counted to ten, and an ox searched for, caught, ridden home, forgotten, until a man walks into the market with open hands. Pure Land: a monk named Dharmakara making vows for a land where all can wake, with birds whose songs are the teaching. Tibet: the ancient ones and the whispered lineage, Milarepa, sending and taking on the breath, monks debating in a courtyard with a clap and a stamp. Other schools and movements: Tiantai and Huayan, the golden lion, Ambedkar's new vehicle, practice put to work for peace and the earth. The schools side by side: the arahant and the bodhisattva, each honored in its own home. The practice traditions: chanting in Pali and to a wooden drum, bowing, a ten-day retreat, a pilgrimage. The festivals: a lamp, a footprint, a pinch of barley, a monk in a pine tree. School after school, each in its own words.
screen: `THE MIND IN MOMENTS.` · `THE SUTRAS: DIAMOND, LOTUS, VIMALAKIRTI.` · `ZEN, PURE LAND, TIBET, THE MOVEMENTS.` · then, large: `CHANT, BOW, RETREAT, FESTIVAL.`

segments.voice: Let a few schools pass through one short sitting: back straight and thumbs just touching, the way Zen sits, and a few out-breaths counted, one to ten. Notice one moment of mind arise and pass, the way the Abhidhamma watches, and, if it feels right, breathe in someone's trouble and breathe out ease, as the Tibetan block taught. Then drop every method and just sit.
The year in one sitting. Year four, seen whole: the Abhidhamma, the great sutras, Zen, Pure Land, Tibet, the movements, the practices and the festivals. Today's word.
screen: `THE YEAR IN ONE SITTING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: look how far. A mango, a burning house, an ox, a bird, a clap in a courtyard. Tomorrow, the year closes.

screen: `DAY 1425 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR FOUR CLOSE: THE SCHOOLS.`

1426.title: Year four close: the schools
1426.hook: many schools, taught in their own words, none ranked
1426.howItsDone: A Buddhist may practice within one school and its teachers and still visit other temples, join gatherings across schools, or keep shared festivals alongside Buddhists of other schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole year in one sitting. Your line was look how far.

On one street in some big cities, you can pass a Thai temple with a gold-tipped roof, a Zen center in a converted house with shoes lined up by the door, a Chinese temple where the name of Amitabha is chanted, and a Tibetan center with prayer flags strung over the porch. Different doors, different shoes at each one. To a newcomer, they can look like four separate religions. Today, the last day of year four, they open onto rooms you've spent a year walking through.
screen: `A GOLD-TIPPED ROOF.` → `SHOES BY A ZEN DOOR.` → `PRAYER FLAGS OVER A PORCH.`

segments.voice: First, the doors. Each school came in by its own door, in its own words. The Theravada's Abhidhamma, taking the mind apart moment by moment. The Mahayana sutras, with their burning houses and rooms full of seats. Zen: sit down and see. Pure Land: call the name and trust. The Tibetan schools, with renunciation, compassion and the diamond path all at once. Tiantai and Huayan, Nichiren and Won, Ambedkar's new vehicle, and teachers carrying it all into hospitals and forests. Second: none of them was ranked. Not because the schools agree on everything. They don't. They differ on which texts are the Buddha's word, on sudden or gradual awakening, on the arahant and the bodhisattva, on what the Pure Land is. Each answers for itself, with its own teachers and reasons. This path's job was to let each one speak, and to say who says what. As day thirteen seventy-eight put it, each one has carried people across. Third, the house. Behind all those doors, this year kept finding the same rooms. The four truths. The three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha. Precepts, meditation, kindness. A bow, a breath, a lamp. A verse about avoiding harm, doing good and clearing the mind, carried on a full moon in Thailand and up a pine tree in China. Many doors: the schools, each whole in itself. One house: the ground they stand on together, which each school would describe in its own words. Fourth: year five opens with a little Pali, the language of the Theravada canon and its chants, then the sources themselves, read slowly, with a path to live.
screen: `MANY DOORS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.` · `NONE RANKED, DIFFERENCES NAMED.` · `THE SHARED ROOMS BEHIND THEM.` · then, large: `MANY DOORS, ONE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Turn toward the nearest door or window and let your eyes rest on it without naming anything. Think of all the doors this year opened, without choosing between them, and let them stand open. Then let your attention go out through the nearest one, over the street, the roofs, the sky, and when it's ready, back to the breath, here, inside the house.
Year four close. The end of the year of the schools: the Abhidhamma, the Mahayana sutras, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions and the movements, each in its own words, none ranked. Today's word.
Your line: many doors, one house. Each school whole in itself, and none ranked. Year four, complete.
